title: Gateless Barrier, Case 40: Kuei-shan Kicks Over the Water Bottle
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk emphasizes the importance of stripping away ego and attachments to gain a deeper understanding of reality. Through stories like Kuishan's rejection of his own ego and Bodhidharma's students' superficial grasping, the teacher highlights how traditional Zen training uses humor and ridicule to help students let go of their preconceptions. By embracing complexity and nuance, we can approach issues like racism and social inequality with a more profound understanding that goes beyond simplistic categorizations.

sentences.text: I've got the recording on.
*An unsurpassed, penetrating and perfect dharma is rarely met with, even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Hopefully I'll have enough of a voice left to give a talk.
Good to see you.
Some of us are being very stalwart, coming here right after the retreat.
It's nice to just maintain continuity, so it's good that we're here.
Although I admit a little moment of resistance in the middle of the afternoon: oh, now we've got to do this again.
But it's good, and it's challenging, right?
Because the world feels a little upside down right now.
On the one hand, it seems like when the world feels upside down, we should respond.
We should drop everything and change our approach, which is probably true enough.
But on the other hand, I was thinking, whatever was solid and stable and helpful yesterday, when the world didn't seem as upside down, or three months ago or whenever, is probably still useful.
So I tucked myself into keeping going with the Mumankan.
And plus, in the sesshin, Norman was using koans too.
Although I noticed he'd start with the koan and then we wouldn't hear about the koan again for quite a while.
So it's interesting the way he used them.
But these [unclear: "end stories"] are really something, aren't they?
They speak to us in surprising ways sometimes.
And when we explore them, it seems like they often do help us to shift perspective and see things differently.
I think part of their nature, too, is that they're operating from a little different frame than our usual way of looking at reality.
When you first read them, they do seem really opaque, and quirky and weird.
So you have to do this whole process with the Zen stories, the Zen koans, of really entering into the middle of them and exploring them and looking from the inside out.
Somehow that just keeps happening each time I crack one of these open.
At first I'm like, eh, another one of these darn Zen stories.
And then you explore around a little while and you go, oh, hmm.
So anyway, we'll see if that happens again.
This is case 40 of the Mumankan.
There are 48 total, so I've entered the 40s.
So here's the story.
We've entered the 40s.
You've been along for the ride.
Case 40.
*When Kuishan, Kuishan, no, Kuishan, Kuishan.
I think it's Kuishan, I must spell it.
When Kuishan was in Baizhong's assembly, he was the tenzo of the monastery.
And Master Baizhong wanted to choose a founding teacher for a new monastery on Mount Takwe.
So he invited all the monks to give a presentation, saying the outstanding one will be sent to be the founding teacher of this new place.*
*Then Master Baizhong took a water bucket and set it on the floor and said, "Don't call this a water bucket.
What would you call it?"
The shuso stood up and said, "It can't be called a wooden clog."
And then Baizhong, the teacher, asked Kuishan his opinion.
Kuishan kicked over the water bucket and walked out.
Baizhong laughed and said, "The shuso loses."
Kuishan was invited to be the founding teacher of this new monastery on Mount Takwe.*
Kuishan is a monk and Baizhong is the teacher.
And there's another monk who is the shuso.
*When Kuishan was in Baizhong's assembly, he was the tenzo of the monastery.
And Master Baizhong wanted to choose a founding teacher for a new monastery on Mount Takwe.
So he invited all the monks to give a presentation, saying the outstanding one will be sent.
Then he took a water bucket and set it on the floor and said, "Don't call this a water bucket.
What do you call it?"
The shuso said, "It can't be called a wooden clog," like a shoe.
And Baizhong then asked Kuishan his opinion.*
*Kuishan just kicked over the water bucket and walked out.
And Baizhong laughed and said, "The shuso loses."
Kuishan was invited to be the founding teacher on Mount Takwe.*
Poor shuso, huh?
Those of us who have been the shuso can relate to this.
Shuso loses.
You're always going to say something wrong, because you're up in front, the one who's supposed to say things when the teacher calls.
So his answer is rejected and he's laughed at by the teacher.
And there is a kind of [unclear: "plan"] of ego-stripping in Zen training.
This traditional way of ridiculing people can, over the long haul, accomplish a beneficial act, actually, of helping people to be more open and flexible and less egoistic.
But it's hard for it to really work without damaging people.
I don't know if they had much of a sense of psychology back in those days.
So we try not to ridicule people at Red Cedar, if we can avoid it.
But still, I think it's worth not throwing that particular baby out, that there is something powerful and important in Zen training.
And we just try to do it more slowly and gently and let it happen organically.
To where we let go a little bit from our attachment to our roles and our big important selves and our opinions and our being right.
Because we know that's all kind of a sham anyway, right, in our heart of hearts.
And we know that it gets in the way.
It gets in the way of connection, it gets in the way of relationships, and it gets in the way of awakening.
So there's an element of that in here, although it's presented in the sort of hardcore – he didn't hit the shoe so anyway – but it's presented in that hardcore, intense way of stripping away ego.
And it's also like this recruiting story.
Strange kind of job interview.
Don't call this a water bucket.
What do you call it?
The right answer, you get the job.
Well, it turns out that the teacher in the story, Bai Zhang, who, by the way, was a very famous and important teacher, is probably in the top 10 or top 20 of the teachers of this era.
Bai Zhang is credited with creating the first monastic rules.
He probably didn't really do that historically, but he's credited with it.
And as I mentioned before, that's a unique and important part of Zen training as well.
It ties into this idea of stripping away the ego, living in a very prescribed, rule-bound way, so that there's no wiggle room, no personal preference, no choice.
You just have to deal with it.
Maybe there's some overlap to the military, I'm sure.
But anyway, Bai Zhang is famous for organizing that kind of monastery early on.
He supposedly lived in the late sixth century.
But it turns out there's a backstory to this little recruitment tale.
The backstory is that Bai Zhang had a friend with some sort of esoteric spiritual powers, like an oracle.
One commentary I read called his friend a geomancer.
Another one called him a psychic.
Anyway, this friend came for a visit a little before this koan story and told Bai Zhang that a nearby mountain called Mount Takwe would be a great location for a new monastery.
Propitious location, right orientation, right shape of the peak.
Somehow, if a monastery was there, it would be really a powerful spiritual place.
I think we all have some agreement that there's something to that kind of thing, right?
Some places do have a certain something.
Like the Samish Island location of our church camp, right?
There's a certain something to that.
It's not just that it's pretty.
And we have all kinds of theories about it.
But anyway, Bai Zhang's friend has feelings for this kind of thing and he tells him, you need to start a monastery up there.
So here's the backstory.
Bai Zhang asks his friend, "Well, who should I send to start this new monastery?
Should I send myself?"
And his psychic friend said, "No, you're too little and too ascetic.
It's a broad mountain and it needs someone large and vigorous."
And just then the shuso, the head monk, came in, and Bai Zhang asked his friend, "Well, how about him?"
So his psychic friend turned to the shuso and asked him to demonstrate how he coughs.
The shuso must have lifted his eyebrows, but he coughed.
And then the psychic asked the shuso to take a few steps.
The shuso did, and the psychic concluded, "No, no, not qualified."
So then in the backstory, Bai Zhang sent for his other senior monk, Kui Shan, the tenzo.
And tenzo is a high, important position.
You have to be a monk a long time before you become a tenzo.
As soon as the psychic saw Kui Shan, he announced, "Here he is.
This is the monk from Mount Ta Kuei."
Bai Zhang agreed and in a private interview told Kui Shan that he was selected for this new job.
But when word got out, the head monk protested.
He represents ego, right?
He protested, saying he was the leader of the students and the head student, leader of the sangha, so he should get the job.
And so, in order to keep the peace, Bai Zhang arranged a contest.
So the contest is our koan.
Although on the face of it, it doesn't really sound like much of a contest, does it?
A little more like a charade, which just confirmed the decision he'd already made.
So that's a powerful thing to wonder.
Is everything a rigged game?
Is it all decided?
Even in job selection in Zen monasteries, much less elections and promotions and all kinds of selection.
It's not who you are, but who you know, all that.
Or is there some real discernment of something important here?
Even though on the face of it, it just seems like a funny little charade.
So Bai Zhang, in the story, took a water bucket and set it on the floor and said, "Don't call this a water bucket.
What would you call it?"
I'm not sure if it matters, but there must be some ambiguity in the characters for water bucket.
I think they would be pretty clear because they're nouns, but I have four different translations, and they variously call it a water bucket, a water bottle, a water jug, and a piss pot.
The story reads a little different if it's a piss pot, I guess.
Chamber pot.
But I decided to go with water bucket.
I don't know if it matters.
I think what matters is that it's an object.
He sets an object out and says, if you don't call this by its name, what would you call it?
Or in other words, how would you understand this object if you don't just use its name and the connected concept that you have for this object?
So the shuso is really quite correct, right, when he says it can't be called a wooden clog.
It is wooden, but it's not a clog, it's not a shoe.
You'd really struggle walking up to this new mountain site if you used buckets for shoes.
But still, this shuso is staying in the same realm, right?
He's staying in the realm of objects.
He's just saying, well, I can't really say what it is, but I can say it's not this other object.
Which is true enough, but not enough.
Not far enough, not deep enough.
So the [unclear: "victorious quesion"] kicks over the bucket and keeps going.
The symbolism here is that reality is too rich and complex for us to ever really understand what an object or anything else truly is.
Our minds can't help but try to narrow things down and use words and concepts as handy handles, handy signs we hang on things so that we can function.
But something is lost.
Something really important is lost when we do that.
And we do it so often and so continuously that we don't realize we're losing so much by living within the realm of words, concepts, and objects.
And even internal stuff is also seen as objects, right?
Mental objects, they are.
But every time we just stay and don't go further than the concept, we miss something.
We can think about the something in the realm of objects and already realize we're missing a lot, even within the realm of objects.
Like when the bucket's knocked over, the object we call water pours out.
So then we say it's an empty bucket.
But actually it's a bucket full of air now, right?
So it's also a full bucket.
Is it empty?
Is it full?
Who can say?
So even staying within the realm of objects, we realize we're simplifying and missing it.
But knocking over the bucket represents freedom from all this.
Saying we can't know what this is.
It's an object and it's beyond an object.
It's a representation and it's connected to the whole universe.
Like it said in that lovely little hymn that we chant:
*She brings light into stress because she understands the own being of all dharmas,*
that things aren't separate objects.
That's a liberative quality, to feel and understand and really deeply see the connections between everything.
And it's not just a bucket, it's the whole universe.
But we do tend to assume that everything has a singularity, right?
A certain objective reality.
This is a water bucket.
This is a shoe.
They're different.
And in those cases, we can get away with that just fine, because with many things our shared collective agreement is so close to 100 percent that we all think it's absolutely true.
Very few people don't see a shoe and call it a shoe or see a bucket and call it a bucket.
If they do, we say there's something wrong with them, and we don't think there's anything wrong with our concepts.
But the big issues that we're grappling with now in our society, that have everything upside down, don't seem to function as easily as buckets and shoes.
They don't seem to sort themselves out as easily into clear, identifiable, agreed-upon categories and realities.
Our world is turning on things that we can't see and we can't agree on and we can't really even understand.
So I'm thinking of the virus and I'm thinking of racism, of course.
The virus is obvious even in the object world, right?
We can't see or understand it, but it does seem to be some kind of object.
But how about concepts like resisting arrest or appropriate force or commensurate force?
These are objects too.
These are concepts.
And one person's way of looking at them and understanding these objects, these concepts, could be so different from someone else's, it's as if they're on a different planet, right?
That one person's understandable nervousness at being arrested after a friendly half-hour chat with a few officers and freaking out a little bit, right?
That's one person's concept.
The other person's concept is resisting arrest and threat, right?
And the guns come out, and one of those people is now dead.
So this is serious, how we look at objects, how we understand concepts.
It's not just about buckets and shoes and old funny stories.
We are so limited by our belief that reality is cut and dry.
That it's this way because I see that it is this way.
It's so hard and upsetting for us to ever even consider that there are other ways of seeing it, or that the object is not as stable as we think it is.
And that there are other people who see it as a completely different object.
Just like the idiot who doesn't recognize a shoe or a bucket, we tend to call the people who don't recognize what we think of as resisting arrest or understandable nervousness idiots, right?
We think of them as idiots.
So it's not that different.
And are we really all that different from the shuso with his smug answer, "I know how to deal with this.
Well, it's not a wooden shoe"?
Nyogen Senzaki, the Japanese teacher who settled in LA that I love so much, said that the shuso had, quote, "always carried the sign head monk pasted on his forehead."
I guess he'd been a head monk for a long time, so he got really prideful.
It's like he has this sign, head monk, pasted on his forehead.
And that really limited his ability to be flexible and see things in any kind of new way.
So that made me wonder how thoroughly I carry a sign on my forehead.
I don't know what it would say.
Liberal middle class educated white guy, maybe, or something.
And that's been on my forehead so long I don't even see it, right?
I don't even know it's there.
How does that limit my options for understanding the way things really are?
How much does that cause me to see certain objects in a certain way and believe that to be reality?
So maybe we really have to figure out more ways to knock over the water buckets, to knock over our concepts, and encourage and invite and make space, right?
Knocking over a bucket in a Dharma talk is kind of dramatic, but it makes space for a new conversation.
And I always assume that the backstory of all these koans is that this was the one weird exception for that decade.
That every other week the Dharma talk was very staid and very scripted and happened exactly the same way, right?
That was because of Bai Zhang's many rules for the monastery.
So our little collection of stories are the wacky time that people talked about for, well, centuries later, because here we are.
So doing it differently, knocking over the water bucket, creates room for a new conversation.
I don't exactly know how we do that with racism and privilege and all this, but we're trying.
And I'm trying, and I seem to be in the speaker's seat here a lot.
So I want to say thank you.
I got a few really interesting comments over email about the Ta-Nehisi Coates article I read excerpts of last week.
If you weren't here, there's a recording of it.
Thank you, Ken, for getting that up.
What a powerful article that is, about the way African Americans were kept off of the great American wealth escalator of home ownership in the twentieth century.
And apologies, by the way, if I didn't respond to what you sent me.
I just got busy with sesshin and thought we could discuss it together anyway.
Because when I read that, it really knocked over my water bucket.
I was shocked by my ignorance.
And maybe some of you who were listening, and people who were here last week, were a little shocked too.
There was a kind of heavy feeling after I spoke.
Maybe you were a little surprised that I didn't already know all that, shocked in a different way.
I've got that sign on my forehead.
And as we learn about this, we really start to recognize, I think, that it's very layered, right?
It's very complex.
That idea of layers keeps coming back to me: layers of knowing, peeling the onion, levels of realization.
That article came out in 2014, so it's been sitting around six years waiting for me.
But I'm reading it now, while the nation is full of protesting after having seen the images.
I haven't chosen to watch the video of [unclear: "Dick Chauvin"] of the Minneapolis police kneeling on George Floyd for nine minutes until he died.
Reading that and noticing all this happening now,
it knocked over my bucket in a way it probably wouldn't have as much another time.
It was interesting to me before.
I want to know about this stuff.
But the bucket can still stay upright when you're just interested.
So I was thinking about this more from my personal life point of view.
That's a good way, I think, for all of us to think about this stuff: get it out of abstraction and into our actual story.
I was realizing, on the educated part of my sign, that my parents were able to help with my college fees partly because of the benefits that they and their parents and their grandparents
received, although that's probably right when the federal [unclear: "back mortgage"] started.
So I'm not sure about my great grandparents.
But anyway, several generations in my family had received all these benefits from being included in the home ownership wealth escalator that he described in that article.
And it's all kinds of weird circumstances, too.
It's not just our whiteness.

Also, the Santa Clara Valley of the San Francisco Bay Area, during the last few generations before me, changed from fruit orchards into suburban housing, and the invention of the suburbs happened, and offices
and then it became the biggest center for technology and wealth the world has ever seen.
I happened to grow up there, and my mom decided to leave being a middle school teacher, where she was pretty miserable, and take up being a real estate agent in 1976.
And for sure, my mom worked hard.
I remember how hard she worked.
She had to really apply her gumption and her intelligence, and I'm sure she was subject to plenty of sexism.
So it's partly up to her.
It was partly the incredible situation that she happened to be in.
It enabled me to be in the situation I'm in.

And meanwhile, just a few years before that, we now know about Clyde Ross in Chicago, working three jobs so he could make payments on a predatory private loan, which was the only way he could buy his house.
Well, my mom and her clients all had FHA-backed mortgages at reasonable rates and terms.
And I was reflecting on this some more, and I realized that there was real estate discrimination in California, for sure, and in the Bay Area, but not as awful as it was in Chicago.
But still, it did exist.
And I'm curious to ask my mom about this more.
I'm going to talk to her on Saturday, which is her birthday.
In our area, black people were steered to the crumbier, high-crime neighborhoods, for sure.
Palo Alto, where I mostly grew up, has a neighboring city called East Palo Alto.
East Palo Alto's downtown is right across this little teeny creek called San Francisquito Creek, which is in a concrete creek bed now.
You go over this little bridge across the creek, and suddenly it's like you're in a different world.
The faces all turn from white to black, the cars are more rundown, the streets look different.
There might not have been sidewalks.
It's amazing.
And the shopping district goes from copy shops and boutiques and bookstores to almost all liquor stores.
The whole area was called Whiskey Gulch.
And Whiskey Gulch grew up to serve people from Stanford University who wanted to get cheap alcohol for the parties.
Maybe there's some tie-in to prohibition, I don't know.
So that didn't happen by accident.
A white town and a black town right next to each other.
Although I assume the residents of East Palo Alto who owned their homes did have normal mortgages, unlike Clyde Ross and his neighbors in Chicago.
Although I sure wouldn't be surprised if they didn't get quite as good an interest rate as their white Palo Alto neighbors.
So I'm curious to find out more.
I remember being surprised by this growing up, but it was also normal, right?
It's just how it was.
It's just what the water bucket looked like.
Palo Alto is this way, East Palo Alto is that way.
East Palo Alto is dangerous, poor, crime there, where the drug dealers lived.
So we all know the bucket of racism to some extent, and I'm sure I do.
I know it's not a wooden shoe, but I don't think I've really kicked over the bucket.
I think there's a long way for me, and maybe for all of us, to really get this in our bones.
And that made me think of another famous Zen story, which is probably a good directive for us about how deeply we need to study this stuff if we really want to be helpful to the world.
This is a story of when Bodhidharma was ready to retire, the legendary Bodhidharma.
We always chant his name.
So he's ready to retire and pass on his Dharma to his best student.
Another great Zen [unclear: "selection story"].
There's a bunch of them.
And the great Bodhidharma had all of four students, actually.
That was the size of his sangha.
So our little gathering tonight is bigger than that.
So here's the story.
Bodhidharma asked his sangha, "Can each of you say something to demonstrate your understanding?"
The first student, Daofu, stepped forward and said, "It is not bound by words and phrases, nor is it separate from words and phrases.
This is the function of the way."
Bodhidharma said, "You have attained my skin."
Then the nun, Zongchur, stepped up and said, "It's like a glorious glimpse of the realm of [unclear: "Asgyoba"] Buddha.
Seen once, it need not be seen again."
Bodhidharma said, "You have attained my flesh."
And the third student, Daoyu, said, "The four elements are empty.
The five skandhas are without actual existence.
Not a single dharma can be grasped."
Bodhidharma said, "You have attained my bones."
Finally, Weka came forth, bowed deeply in silence, and stood up straight.
Bodhidharma said, "You have attained my marrow."
So in this story, Weka is the one who knocks over the bucket.
So that's pretty good, how you heard this story before: skin, flesh, bones, marrow.
And one cool note I hear is that of Bodhidharma, great first ancestor of China's, four students, one of them is a nun.
So there were women from the beginning, no question.
At least a few of them were mentioned in the stories.
Not enough though.
Anyway, the African-American folks that we share our great country with, for sure have racism in their marrow.
And we're probably feeling the outlines of it on our skin, or a little bit in our flesh, depending on our history.
I feel like it's very much just skin deep for me.
And I suspect this makes it really difficult to have a real conversation.
If we all think we're talking about the same thing,

racism, water buckets, whatever it is, and some of us understand it in one way, in our skin and our flesh, and others understand it in a deeper way, in their bones and their marrow, it's hard to be on the same page, right?
It's hard to have a really meaningful conversation.
It's easy to talk over and around each other.
And of course, our leaders right now, it's truly hard to watch, isn't it?
All of our leaders say, and I'm sure they're not lying, I believe this, that they're not racist.
We have that written on all of our foreheads, right?
If we don't have it in our marrow, we write it on our foreheads instead.
And in between the retreat and this evening, I did have the news on briefly, and I had the pleasure of watching a few minutes of the House or the Senate.
Oh, I guess it must have been the Senate.
Yeah, a Senate committee studying what to do about policing, because Kamala Harris and Cory Booker were chairing the meeting, and they were inviting African American professors and wise folks in.
So I saw a little bit of the exchange, and yeah, really deep and powerful.
It's definitely some bones and marrow being expressed in the great U.S.
Senate, so that's encouraging.
But it takes more than talk, right?
It takes more than talk.
It takes deep practice, it takes transformation, and it takes more than just inviting in the people who have it in their bones and their marrow to share.
For the people who only have it in their skin and their flesh, it doesn't sink in.
It doesn't sink in as deeply as it needs to.
Maybe one day it will.
So anyway, all this to say, we're lucky we have all this support to look deeply and study deeply, as Dogen and all these ancestors are constantly encouraging us.
It's not just a water bucket, right?
It's not just the idea "I'm not a racist."
It's not just skin color.
It's deeper.
And what can we do but just take the next step?
Start heading up the mountain.
See if we can start a monastery that's deeper than just calling a bucket a bucket or a shoe a shoe.
To have Red Cedar be a place and a community of real healing and transformation as best we can.
So that's my thought for tonight.
Maybe we did manage to milk something useful
out of Master Bai Zhang's funny little [unclear: "selection story"].
It does seem like the shuso had no chance, doesn't it?
And then the other thing about buckets is that buckets are also an important metaphor for awakening.
When you pick up the bucket and it's still holding all the water, it's incomplete.
What you're hoping will happen one day is that the bottom falls out.
So there's another bucket metaphor.
Maybe eventually the bottom will fall out and we'll all wake up.
